extracted.intended_audience: patent scholars, patent practitioners, judges, policymakers, and law students interested in patent scope and policy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and normative criteria for assessing and constraining the proper scope of patent claims (enablement, equivalents, product vs process, pioneer patents), with attention to industry differences (biotechnology, chemical, cumulative technologies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent scope should not exceed inventor's disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: It is basic to the grant of a patent that the scope of a patent should not exceed the scope of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and the Patent Office should restrain claim breadth to what the inventor actually invented and taught in the specification; avoid granting broad claims that cover embodiments well beyond the patent's disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement and written description constraint (35 U.S.C. §112)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must contain a written description and enablement in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to make and use the invention, and must set forth the best mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequacy of disclosure is measured as of the filing date; failure to disclose best mode or to enable the claimed scope can invalidate or limit claims (illustrated by Genentech/Scripps and other cases). Enablement doctrine should limit claim breadth to what is actually taught.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalents inquiry should assess accused device's degree of advance
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a court assesses the significance of the patented device, it should also consider the importance of the advance represented in the accused device when applying the doctrine of equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should examine whether the accused device shows major differences from the patented device — focusing on differences in materials; changes in the number of components; greatly improved efficiency in individual components; and increased efficiency in how components work together (overall design improvements). The Texas Instruments approach is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse doctrine of equivalents (defense for significant improvements)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an improvement represents a very significant advance, it should be held not to infringe even if it is within the literal bounds of the patentee's claim (reverse equivalents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply reverse equivalents liberally, especially when the allegedly infringing improvement embodies new technology not available when the patent issued. Reverse equivalents are an important tool to prevent blocking by pioneer patents (examples: Westinghouse, Hughes Satellite, polypropylene cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict overly broad pioneer patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Pioneer patents are often granted broad scope that can block subsequent inventors; there is frequently no justification for the breadth granted and upheld.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Office and courts should pay close attention to what the pioneer inventor actually disclosed and what was already in the public domain; trim claims to reflect the actual contribution and avoid blocking follow-on innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust scope based on industry character (science-based vs cumulative vs discrete)
rubrics_metrics.description: The appropriate scope of patents depends on industry characteristics: science-based industries and cumulative technologies are especially vulnerable to over-broad early patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious awarding broad patents early in science-based industries (e.g., biotechnology, superconductors). In cumulative technologies broad component patents can cause blockages; scope doctrines should be sensitive to these differences and tailored accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer process (or product-by-process) claims for purified natural products and obvious variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Product patents on purified forms of natural substances or on structurally obvious variants can block subsequent recombinant or improved processes/products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granting process patents or product-by-process claims is more consistent with enablement and better reflects what the inventor actually achieved; this reduces blocking of improvements (illustrated by Parke-Davis/adrenalin and Scripps/Genentech).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit product patents for new uses of known compounds; favor method patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Because a product patent covers all uses, granting product patents for new uses of old compounds creates confusion and enforcement problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a compound is structurally obvious from prior art but has a newly discovered use or property, protection should be limited to method/process patents directed to the new use/property to avoid granting a 17-year monopoly on the substance itself; enforcement challenges should be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Office scrutiny of claims vis-à-vis public domain and specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Office should pay closer attention to the inventor's specification and the broad nature of what was already known and in the public domain when deciding claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrict allowed claim scope accordingly to avoid granting monopolies over what was already part of public science or what the inventor did not actually teach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness and prior publications should limit claim breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that would be obvious in light of prior publications or prior art should be rejected; prior publication can render claims obvious and prevent overly broad patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use obviousness analysis to deny broad, prospect-like patents (example: rejection of an overly broad gene expression patent because inventors published results prior to the claimed invention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing and cross-licensing are mitigations but not justifications for broad patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-licensing and patent pools have been used to resolve blockages caused by broad patents but they are mechanisms to work around blocking power rather than reasons to grant broad patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on industry licensing practices as a normative justification for awarding broad patents; licensing may mitigate blocking effects but does not demonstrate social efficacy of broad scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor scope doctrines to preserve incentives for subsequent improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Scope doctrines can be used to approximate an optimal patent breadth that preserves incentives for both pioneers and subsequent improvers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrinal modifications (narrowing of broad claims, use of reverse equivalents, strict adherence to disclosure) should be applied judiciously and primarily to a small number of pioneering breakthroughs to retain incentives for initial inventions while protecting follow-on innovation.
